#13Summary conclusion

Pernod Ricard is a strong brand portfolio with earnings at a trough and shares at the lowest multiple in ten years. The worry about distributors cutting stock is starting to clear, but the balance sheet still needs fixing. The investment case is therefore a re-rating and income case, with an option on the company keeping more of its cost savings; it is not yet an earnings-upgrade case.

Where the case standsThe case is moderately strong on price and weak on earnings momentum. Certainty is low until the first-half results on 18-Feb-27 show which way the savings and the US shipments are going.

What to watch, in order of importance.

  1. 18-Feb-27, first-half FY27 results: the US organic decline (it should narrow towards (5)%), the organic operating margin together with the advertising ratio, net debt at December 2026, and whether the company holds its FY27 guidance
  2. Monthly US state-store and scanner data: Pernod's growth gap to the US spirits market at (2) points or better, and the trend in price and mix
  3. The board's decision on the Indian listing, and the rulings on Indian tax, the Delhi licence and the tariff on bulk Scotch
  4. April 2027, third-quarter sales: how much of the sales pulled forward ahead of the German and Polish excise rises is given back, and how China traded after Chinese New Year
  5. Late August 2027, FY27 results: FY28 guidance, the medium-term sales target, the dividend and the scrip

Memo ratings.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 41, set by the Rater. The external forces are a net negative (operating environment, topic #1, scored 34): US consumption and prices are falling and China sales have halved, and the only positive is the one-off relief of destocking ending. Large cost self-help (corporate change, topic #2, scored 59) offsets the external forces, but forecasts already largely absorb the savings. The financial output does not improve enough: earnings per share grow about 2.4% a year from a trough, and margins stay below their past levels (forecast financials, grade D). The net change is mildly negative, and the positive change that exists reaches profit only through costs, so the rating sits in the low 40s.

Foundations' Robustness: 60, set by the Rater. The quality of the business (topic #3, scored 61) rests on aged stock and brands that are hard to copy, and on an operating margin that held at 26% to 28% through a 22% fall in sales; that margin record shows real stability in the profit pool. Four weaknesses hold the rating to about 60: lost market share in the United States and China, the highest debt among peers, a dividend that absorbs the cash, and a three-year record of missed sales guidance (topic #4, scored 40). Pernod sits with Judges Scientific and Nexans: protected franchises let down by recent delivery.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 62, set by the Rater. The case matches the entry conditions of the setup 'Major Cause for Concern Clearing in a Medium-Quality non-cyclical or better business on a first-quartile multiple': the multiple is at the 1st percentile, the concern is named (destocking and debt), the tests are dated, and the first test was passed. Today's problems in the business loosen the fit. Continuing US share loss and falling consumption leave open whether the concern is cyclical excess stock or structurally weaker demand, and therefore whether there is a 'normal' level of earnings to revert to. The rating sits in the middle of Richard's 65-75 range for a concern clearing in a middling business, less a little for those current problems; the missing upgrades are a matter of timing and are not counted here.

Case Riskiness: 38, set by the Rater. The riskiness and simplicity score (topic #9, scored 36) is driven by five linked drivers resting on leverage of 3.8 times EBITDA, a dividend with no cover beyond the scrip, unhedged currency, and Indian legal and trade rulings that can arrive suddenly, all with a downward-skewed range for earnings per share. Most of the risk is slow-moving and trackable, and the 1st-percentile multiple limits the de-rating risk that Richard weighs for a large share-price fall. Those two points lift the rating slightly above topic #9's score, but Pernod remains a complex, geared case, below typical on riskiness.

#0The investment case

1. The one idea. Pernod Ricard owns spirits brands (Jameson, Martell, Chivas, Absolut, Ballantine's and about 200 more) and collects the brand owner's share of the spirits value chain: a gross margin near 58% and an operating margin near 26%. Pernod earns that share by spending about 16% of sales on advertising, by financing €7 billion of ageing whisky and cognac, and by selling through distributors it does not control. Three consequences follow from that business model.

  • The competitive position rests on aged stock and brands, which a newcomer cannot copy quickly
  • The main risk is that distributors order less than drinkers buy, for longer than expected, in the two richest markets (the United States and China), while prices are being cut
  • Earnings are geared: most costs do not flex with sales and net debt is 3.7 times EBITDA, so a 1% change in sales moves operating profit by about 1.6% and earnings per share by about 2%

2. The change. Three forces are at work, and all three are relief or self-help, not rising demand.

  • Destocking is ending. In the first quarter of FY27, US shipments fell 10% while Pernod's sales to drinkers ran about 2 points behind a US market that fell 4%; distributors cutting stock therefore explain about 4 points of the shipment fall. China shipments fell 25% while sales to drinkers grew. When shipments merely match consumption again, group organic growth improves by about 2 points, once
  • Costs are coming out. Pernod delivered half of a €1 billion cost programme in FY26; the remaining €500 million, about a fifth of operating profit, is due by FY28
  • India can fix the balance sheet. India is about 13% of group sales and grows at high single digits, and a partial listing of the Indian business could raise about €2.5 billion
  • The headwinds are present, not absent: US spirits sales by value are falling and Pernod is still losing US share; the cost of aged liquid cut gross margin by 221 basis points in FY26; advertising was cut to 15% of sales and must be rebuilt; Europe's sales fell 6% organically in the first quarter; and India carries tax and licence disputes

3. How the change reaches the financials. Organic sales growth moves from about (0.7)% in FY27 to about +2% in FY28, because shipments stop falling faster than consumption. The margin rises only slowly, because the savings must first pay for rebuilt advertising and dearer aged liquid.

  • My earnings per share: €5.69 in FY27, €5.87 in FY28 and €6.11 in FY29, against consensus of €5.70, €5.97 and €6.13, so my forecasts are at or just below consensus
  • Guidance: the FY27 guidance of stable organic sales and a defended margin is most likely to be met, not raised, on 18-Feb-27
  • Sell-side estimates: likely flat to slightly down on the underlying business, with currency the only clear source of upgrades
  • The narrative can move from "the weakest growth since 1975" to "the trough has passed" at the FY27 results in late August 2027, if US shipments have converged on consumption by then

4. The foundation. The assets are high quality, and the present delivery is medium quality.

  • For: the operating margin held between 25.8% and 27.6% while reported sales fell 22% from the FY23 peak; every cost and margin promise has been kept; the family owns about 15% of the shares, and a family company bought €162 million of shares in June 2026
  • Against: sales targets have been missed for three years; Pernod has lost share in US spirits and in Chinese cognac; cash flow after the dividend has been about nil; debt is the highest among the peers

5. The setup. The best-fitting setup is "Major Cause for Concern Clearing in a Medium-Quality non-cyclical or better business on a first-quartile multiple, leading to reversion to normal".

  • Present: a two-year forward multiple at the 1st percentile of ten years (11.8 times); a named cause for concern (destocking and debt) with dated tests; and the first test, the first-quarter sales, passed on 15-Oct-26
  • Missing: proof that the US decline is excess stock and not falling consumption; any upgrades (the dashboard rates sell-side momentum F); and a "normal" level of earnings to revert to, since consensus earnings per share for FY30 (€6.43) is still 19% below FY24 (€7.90)

6. The reward and the skew.

The skewThe skew is positive in the share price and not in the earnings: about +19% probability-weighted over 18 months, from a 1st-percentile multiple and a 6.6% dividend yield.
  • If the case plays out (destocking ends, the Indian listing happens, the shares reach 16 times earnings): about +63% over 18 months
  • On my forecasts (13 times earnings): about +27%, of which 10 points is dividend
  • If the case fails (deeper destocking, a dividend cut, 10 times earnings): about (15)%
  • Probability-weighted: about +19% over 18 months
  • At the guideline fair multiple of 21.87 times, the arithmetic gives about +106%, which I think is very unlikely inside 18 months
  • Against Richard's test: Pernod is not a case where upgrades are unusually skewed to the positive. The case is a low multiple and a 6.6% yield with an option on the worry clearing. Evidence that the company is keeping its savings as profit would create a stronger case

7. What has to be true. Three conditions must hold, and the first-half results test all three.

  • US shipments converge on consumption without more lost share: the first-half results on 18-Feb-27 should show the US decline narrowing from (10)% towards (5)%, and monthly state-store and scanner data should hold Pernod's gap to the market at (2) points or better
  • Savings reach profit without starving the brands: on 18-Feb-27 the organic operating margin should be flat or up, with advertising at 15% to 16% of sales, not below
  • The balance sheet is fixed without cutting the dividend: the board approves the Indian listing (no date in my files), and net debt is at or below 3.7 times EBITDA at December 2026
18-Feb-27
The date that matters: first-half FY27 results. The first-half results test all three conditions at once: the US decline, the margin with advertising held, and net debt at December 2026.

The judgements that move the value of the shares most

The biggest leverThe multiple moves the value of the shares far more than any earnings judgement: one turn of the multiple is worth 8% to 9% of the share price, while each earnings judgement is worth less than 5%, except a joint 10% adverse currency move.

1. The multiple. Each 1.0 times of multiple, applied to forward earnings per share of about €6.0 to €6.4, is worth about €6 a share, or 8% to 9% of the share price.

  • From 11.8 times to 13 times: +10%
  • From 11.8 times to 14.5 times (the 10th percentile of ten years): +23%
  • From 11.8 times to 10 times (the five-year low is 9.9 times): (15)%

2. FY28 organic sales: does destocking end?

  • 1 point of organic sales growth is €93 million of sales
  • At a drop-through of about 42% (58% gross margin less 16% advertising; my assumption), 1 point of sales is €39 million of operating profit, or 1.6%
  • Interest is fixed at about €425 million, so 1 point of sales moves pre-tax profit by 1.9% and earnings per share by €0.11
  • If FY28 organic growth is 0% and not my 2.2%: (€86) million of operating profit and (€0.25) a share (4)%. If FY28 growth is 4%: +€0.20 a share (+3.5%)

3. How much of the savings is kept.

The unpriced optionConsensus assumes that about 88% of the €500 million of savings still to come is absorbed by costs elsewhere. Keeping more of the savings is the case's main unpriced option.
  • €500 million of savings is still to come by FY28, yet consensus operating profit rises only €61 million from FY26 to FY28, so consensus assumes about 88% of the savings is absorbed
  • If only 70% of the savings is absorbed: +€90 million of operating profit, or +€0.26 a share (+4.4%)
  • If gross margin falls a further 100 basis points: (€95) million of operating profit, or (€0.27) a share (4.6)%

4. The balance sheet: the Indian listing and the dividend.

  • The Indian listing helps the balance sheet far more than earnings. A 20% listing at a value of about €12 billion raises €2.5 billion and cuts net debt by 0.55 to 0.9 times EBITDA, on brokers' estimates. The interest saved at 3.4% is €85 million, but most of that saving is given back as the minority shareholders' share of Indian profit, so earnings per share rise only 1.0% to 1.4% (€0.06 to €0.08). The listing's value therefore shows up in the multiple (judgement 1), not in earnings
  • Without the listing, debt stays above target. My cash forecasts leave net debt near 3.4 times EBITDA at June 2029, against a target of below 3 times: a gap of about €1.2 billion. My files do not say whether the €1.5 billion hybrid bond issued in October 2026 counts as debt in the company's ratio; if the hybrid does not count, the gap closes on paper
  • The dividend takes all the cash. The €4.70 dividend is 83% of FY27 earnings per share and costs about €1.2 billion a year, against my FY27 free cash flow of €1.1 billion. A cut to €3.00 would take 2.4 points a year off the return

5. Currency.

  • A 1% move in the US dollar changes operating profit by €12 million, or earnings per share by €0.035 (0.6%)
  • A joint 10% adverse move in the US dollar, Indian rupee, Chinese yuan and Turkish lira would cost about €270 million, or about 10.6% of earnings per share (Risks report)

#1Operating environment

The messageThe operating environment is getting less bad, not good: the stock correction is ending, while weak consumption and falling prices continue.

Evidence.

  • United States: spirits sales by value in the state-store data fell 7.0% in August 2026 (volume (4.5)%, price and mix (2.5)%), the steepest fall since November 2025. Ready-to-drink volumes grew 23.7% in 2025 while distilled spirits fell 4.1%. The share of US adults who drink alcohol is 54%, a 90-year low
  • China: Pernod's China sales have halved, from €1.4 billion in FY23 to €0.7 billion, with the banqueting and night-time channels held down by official restraint on spending. China settled its anti-dumping case on cognac through minimum import prices, at a cost to Pernod of €45 million over 12 months
  • Europe: excise rises in Germany and Poland in January 2027 pull sales into the second quarter of FY27 and out of the third
  • Helpful factors: the India-UK trade agreement halved the Indian tariff on Scotch to 75% from July 2026, though Indian customs dispute the cut for bulk Scotch, about 80% of what Pernod ships; the United States removed its tariffs on Scotch in April 2026; and currency, which cost €268 million of sales in FY26, cost only €3 million in the first quarter of FY27

Inference and so-what. The environment is getting less bad, not good. What is ending is a correction in distributors' stock; what continues is weak consumption and falling prices. For that reason I credit the recovery to shipments returning to the level of consumption and to cost savings, and I give no credit for price.

Counter-case

US scanner data cover only about 16% of US spirits sales by value and miss bars, so US consumption may be better than the data show. Former executives think the shift to canned cocktails is partly cyclical.

What would change my view

US sales to drinkers of full-strength spirits returning to flat, and US price and mix turning positive.

Against the market

Viewforth's Sector note calls the end of spirits destocking a "Big" worry clearing. I agree on the direction and differ on the speed: the finance chief said the stock adjustments last through FY27, and Redburn expects shipments to match consumption only in FY31.

Conclusion: the tailwinds are weak and one-off, and the headwinds are several and continuing. The operating environment weakens step 2 of the case: the change is relief, so the change supports a re-rating from a very low multiple more than it supports earnings upgrades.

Score: 34, set by the Rater. The external picture is a net negative. Destocking is ending and is worth about 2 points of group growth once, and the US and Indian Scotch tariff relief and neutral currency help a little. Against those positives, US spirits sales by value are falling 7% with price and mix negative, the share of US adults who drink is at a 90-year low, ready-to-drink drinks are taking volume, China sales have halved under official restraint, and European excise moves sales between quarters. Consensus sales growth at the 16th percentile tells the truth here, because the relief is cyclical while the pressure on consumption and price is structural or long-lived. That puts the environment below Entra's mild negative and a little above Vodafone's mature, below-typical environment.

#2Corporate change

The messageThe internal change is large in cost and thin in growth: real, well executed and, so far, defensive.

Evidence.

  • Structure: Pernod merged fifty market companies into ten management entities and eight brand companies into two units. Headcount is down 18% (about 3,600 people) since June 2023, and sales staff are down 12%. Organic structure costs fell 8% in FY26
  • Portfolio: disposals have raised about €1.5 billion. According to Redburn, the sale of Imperial Blue adds about 150 basis points to India's margin, and the exit from US wine adds about 60 basis points to the US margin
  • Balance sheet: Pernod issued €1.5 billion of hybrid bonds in October 2026, and the Indian business is being converted to a public company ahead of a possible listing
  • People and pay: a new finance chief who ran the transformation, a new head of legal and M&A, and a Groupe Bruxelles Lambert director (formerly of KKR) on the board from 20-Nov-26. For FY27 the management bonus replaces the operating-margin criterion with net sales
  • Not done: merger talks with Brown-Forman ended in April 2026

Inference and so-what. The change to the bonus is the most telling item. By paying management for sales instead of margin, the board itself admits that cost-cutting has done what it can. The risk in the new sales incentive is volume bought with lower prices.

Counter-case

Former executives say that morale is damaged, that 200 brands dilute the sales force's focus, and that Diageo has dedicated teams at the largest US distributor where Pernod shares a sales book. The former executives may carry grievances, but the market-share data agree with them.

What would change my view

A first-half operating margin that rises with the advertising ratio restored, and Pernod's US growth gap to the market closed.

Against the market

Brokers treat the savings as fully absorbed. I agree for FY27 and see retention of savings in FY28 as the main unpriced option.

Conclusion: the corporate change is real, well executed on cost and so far defensive. The corporate change supports step 3 of the case on margin and leaves step 3 open on sales.

Score: 59, set by the Rater. The self-help is large and well executed. A EUR 1bn cost programme is half delivered, and the remaining EUR 500m is about a fifth of operating profit; headcount is down 18%, EUR 1.5bn of disposals lift margins, and there is a hybrid bond issue, a planned Indian listing and a new finance chief. But the self-help is repair of a mature business, and consensus treats most of the savings as absorbed by advertising and aged-liquid costs. US share loss, damaged morale and the focus problem of 200 brands are internal offsets, and the bonus switch to sales shows that cost-cutting has done what it can. On the scoring levels, repair-only self-help sits in the low 60s; trimmed for the offsets, Pernod sits between Odfjell and Shell.

#3Foundations

The messagePernod is a medium-quality business today, built on high-quality assets: the brands held the margin through a 22% fall in sales.

Evidence.

  • Industry and value chain: brand owners earn gross margins of 60% to 70%, while distillers and distributors earn far less. Spirits is a fragmented industry (Diageo has 9% of global revenue, Pernod 6%), but US distributors are consolidating and gaining power
  • Competitive advantage: Jameson holds 86% of US Irish whiskey volume; the top four cognac houses hold 90% of cognac; Pernod controls its own distribution in about 60 countries. In the United States Pernod is only fifth, with a 5% share against Diageo's 15.4%
  • Financial profile: Pernod's operating margin of 26% sits below Diageo's (29% to 30%) and above Campari's and Rémy Cointreau's. Return on invested capital is about 11% (the Business Foundations report's estimate) against Diageo's 16% in 2022. Organic sales grew 3% a year from 2019 to 2025, against 8.4% for Campari and 5% for Diageo. Working capital is 77% of sales
  • Management: Alexandre Ricard has led the company since 2015 as chairman and chief executive; the Ricard family holds about 15% of the capital and 22% of the votes. Employee engagement is 88% to 89%. Insiders sold no shares in twelve months. The 2022 medium-term target of 4% to 7% organic growth was missed and has been cut twice. Industry experts describe a centralised inner circle that challenges little

Inference and so-what. Pernod is a medium-quality business today built on high-quality assets. The brands held the operating margin through a severe fall in sales, and that margin record is the strongest evidence of robustness in the file. The financial profile is only average, because ageing stock and the dividend absorb the cash.

Counter-case

If the US decline is share lost to tequila and canned drinks, categories where Pernod is underweight, the assets are worth less than their history says.

What would change my view

Jameson and Absolut gaining US share for two half-years running.

Against the market

Morgan Stanley applies a 25% valuation discount to consumer staples. I think Pernod's assets do not deserve the discount and its balance sheet does, until debt falls.

Conclusion: a favourable industry position and strong brands, an average financial profile, and a management team that delivers on cost and not on sales. The foundations support step 4 of the case, with the sales record as the weak point.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. The value chain is favourable (brand owners take gross margins of 60-70%), and aged stock and brands are real barriers to entry: Jameson has 86% of US Irish whiskey, the top four cognac houses hold 90%, and Pernod owns its distribution in about 60 countries. The operating margin held at 25.8-27.6% through a 22% fall in sales, which shows robustness. Against that, Pernod is only fifth in the United States and is losing share there and in Chinese cognac; structurally moderate drinking and the shift to ready-to-drink cloud the competitive advantage; and management delivers on cost but not on sales. Gross and operating margins are at the 81st and 78th percentiles, but return on invested capital is only 4.5% reported (33rd percentile) and about 11% on the report's basis, with working capital at 77% of sales and debt the highest among peers. So the financial profile is average, and predictability is weaker than a consumer-staples label implies. Pernod sits just below Carlsberg (which has stronger returns and working capital) and just above Helios Towers.

#4Guidance and delivery record

The messagePernod misses on sales and beats on cost and cash, so it is not a habitual upgrader: beats come through cost and are worth 2% to 3% on earnings, not 10%.

Evidence.

  • Sales guidance, missed: FY24 sales were guided to the 4% to 7% medium-term framework and came in at (1.2)% organic. FY26 began as "a year of improvement", was cut in April 2026 to (3)% to (4)%, and came in at (3.9)% against consensus of (3.7)%
  • Profit and cash guidance, met or beaten: FY25 delivered its promised 64 basis points of margin gain. In FY26, operating profit fell 5.2% organically against consensus of (5.9)%, earnings per share were €5.85 against consensus of €5.71, cash conversion was 91% against guidance of about 80%, and the savings came a year early
  • Sell-side: over twelve months, consensus earnings per share fell 11.4% for FY27 and 13.2% for FY28
  • Now: FY27 guidance is for stable organic sales. First-quarter organic sales fell 0.9% against (1.7)% expected, though India's +19% included stock built ahead of the possible listing

Inference and so-what. Pernod's guidance is not conservative on sales and is conservative on cost and cash. Management does not manage expectations down; the sell-side has done that for it. Jefferies, which rates the shares a buy, forecasts (0.8)% organic sales for FY27 against guidance of stable. The bar is therefore low, and beats arrive through cost, which is worth 2% to 3% on earnings, not 10%.

Counter-case

The lowered medium-term target and a new finance chief may mark the first cautious guidance of the current cycle.

What would change my view

Two half-years running with sales at or above guidance.

Against the market

I agree with the market. Deutsche Bank read the FY27 guidance as implying downgrades.

Conclusion: Pernod has a record of delivering profit against lowered bars and of missing on sales, so it is not a habitual upgrader. The delivery record weakens step 3 of the case: the route from change to upgrades runs through costs only.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. Sales guidance has been missed for three years. FY24 came in at (1.2)% organic against a 4-7% framework, FY26 guidance was cut in April and the year still came in below consensus, and the medium-term target has been cut twice, with consensus earnings per share down 11-13% over twelve months. Cost, margin and cash promises were all kept or beaten, though: FY26 earnings per share were EUR 5.85 against EUR 5.71 expected, cash conversion was 91% against about 80% guided, and the savings came a year early. Management does not manage expectations down, and the current guidance of stable sales is not conservative. The record is better than Hexatronic's walk-backs, but the multi-year sales misses keep it below Instalco.

#5Pricing power and gearing

The messagePernod has no pricing power today but high operating and financial gearing: each point of sales becomes about 2% of earnings per share, in both directions.

Evidence.

  • Pricing power is negative for now. In the August 2026 US state-store data, prices were more than 1% lower than a year earlier on 44% of Pernod's US products, against 71% at Diageo and 69% at Rémy Cointreau. Management says that price is no longer a tool for raising the margin
  • Operating leverage is high. Structure costs were €1,663 million, about 18% of sales, and are largely fixed. On my arithmetic, without the savings and the cut in advertising, FY26 operating profit would have fallen by about a quarter on a 3.9% organic fall in sales; with the savings and the advertising cut, operating profit fell 5.2%
  • Financial leverage adds about a fifth to the gearing. Interest is about 18% of operating profit
  • Scope for further cost-cutting remains: €500 million of savings is still due by FY28 (#0)
  • Two feedback loops compete. Cutting advertising protects the margin but loses market share, which invites discounting. Paying down debt lowers interest and brings back the share buyback

Inference and so-what. The gearing that hurt profit on the way down will help on the way up, but only when volume returns in the United States and China, the highest-margin markets. Mix makes the first step of the recovery weaker than the sales line suggests: the first quarter's growth came from India, at lower margins.

Counter-case

A lower fixed-cost base raises the drop-through on any recovery above my 42%.

What would change my view

Positive US price and mix, which would show that brand strength, not discounting, is moving the volume.

Against the market

The sell-side quotes the company's sensitivity of about €24 million of profit per point of sales, which uses the average margin. I think the marginal figure is nearer €39 million, in both directions.

Conclusion: no pricing power today, high operating and financial gearing, and a cost programme currently spent on standing still. The gearing supports step 1 of the case and leaves step 3 dependent on volume.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. Operating gearing is real: fixed structure costs and a marginal drop-through of about 42% mean that 1% of sales moves operating profit about 1.6% and earnings per share about 2%. Financial leverage adds about a fifth, with interest at 18% of operating profit, and EUR 500m of cost savings remains to come. But pricing power is negative for now, with prices cut on 44% of US products, and net debt at 3.7x EBITDA is uncomfortable rather than a comfortable amplifier. The savings are being spent on advertising and dearer aged liquid, and the two feedback loops compete (cutting advertising loses share). Consensus earnings per share grow only about 1.5 times as fast as revenue, below the median of about 2 times. Pernod's gearing is ordinary and asymmetric, with no pricing power behind it, so the score sits at the middle level.

How I tested these forecasts.

  • Does the delivery record make the change plausible? The margin defence rests on a strength the company has shown. The sales recovery rests on a strength the company has not shown for three years. I therefore credit the cost savings and discount the sales recovery
  • How wide is the range of outcomes? Forward earnings per share in 18 months range from about €5.50 to €6.80 around my €6.39: the range is wider below my forecast than above it
  • Is the dividend safe? At 83% of earnings, the dividend is covered in cash only with the scrip option

Inference and so-what. Growth and margins are lower than in the past, not higher. Revenue grows about 1.9% a year and earnings per share about 2.8% a year from FY26 to FY31, and the operating margin stays below the FY22 peak of 28.3%. Double-digit earnings growth appears in only one year of the better case, when the end of destocking, retained savings and the Indian listing coincide.

Counter-case

Bernstein expects earnings growth of 6% a year from FY27 to FY30.

What would change my view

Evidence on 18-Feb-27 that the company is keeping its savings as profit.

Against the market

I am 0.2% below consensus earnings per share for FY27 and 1.7% below for FY28, because I assume organic sales growth about half a point lower each year.

Conclusion: low-single-digit growth from a trough, with the dividend taking almost all the cash. The forecast financials weaken step 3 of the case: the financials recover but do not step up.

#7Scope for upgrades

The weakest linkOn my base case there is no scope for upgrades in the next 6 to 12 months. I count only what is not already in guidance or consensus, and the one large source, retained savings, is unproven.

The earnings events in the next 18 months, with my probabilities.

  • 18-Feb-27, first half of FY27: FY27 guidance met, about 60%; lowered, about 25%; raised, about 15%
  • April 2027, third-quarter sales: likely weak, as the sales pulled forward ahead of the excise rises unwind
  • Late August 2027, FY27 results and FY28 guidance: the "close to 3%" medium-term growth target held, about 60%; lowered, about 35%; raised, about 5%
  • October 2027, February 2028 and April 2028: exact dates not in my files

Consensus over the next two events: held within 1%, about 55%; cut, about 30%; raised, about 15%, most likely because of currency.

Where upgrades could come from that consensus does not hold.

  • Savings retention: worth 4% or more on FY28 earnings per share (judgement 3 in #0). I cannot yet name evidence that the company is keeping the savings, which is why retention is not in my numbers
  • The Indian listing: not in consensus; worth about 1% on earnings per share and more on the multiple
  • Currency: Morgan Stanley raised its near-term earnings forecasts by 4% on currency and lower scrip dilution alone

Inference and so-what. The breadth of revisions can move from negative to neutral as the cuts stop. Breadth turns positive only if the savings are kept or destocking ends early, and there is no evidence yet for either.

Counter-case

Morgan Stanley expects the first quarter's favourable phasing of Asian shipments to unwind, which would mean cuts.

What would change my view

A first-half organic operating margin up 30 basis points or more, with the advertising ratio held.

Against the market

Bernstein and Jefferies see the trough as passed and upgrades to come. I think their call is one or two results early.

Conclusion: the scope for upgrades in the next year is low, and the one large source of upgrades is unproven. Scope for upgrades is the weakest link in the case: it leaves step 3 open and makes step 6 rest on the multiple.

Score: 30, set by the Rater. Guidance counts most, and the memo puts the FY27 guidance at about 25% likely to be lowered on 18-Feb-27 against 15% likely to be raised, and the 'close to 3%' medium-term target at 35% likely to be lowered against 5% raised. Consensus over the next two events is twice as likely to be cut as raised. With revenue growth near zero, even a small cut is a large negative on Richard's ratio. The upside sources (savings retention worth 4% or more on FY28, the Indian listing worth about 1%, and currency) have no evidence yet, and Morgan Stanley expects the first quarter's Asian phasing to unwind. Only the narrative ('the trough has passed') leans up. Downgrades are more likely than upgrades: a little worse than TT Electronics and better than Indutrade, because the narrative and currency can turn.

#8Momentum

The messageThe share price has turned before the estimates. The peer group is turning up, and Pernod is last in the group.

Evidence (dashboard, 23-Nov-26).

  • Pinned ratings: technical momentum D; sell-side earnings momentum F; valuation A
  • Revisions: consensus earnings per share changed 0% over one month, (2)% over three, (3)% over six and (11)% over twelve. The mean target price fell 6% over three months. Buy ratings are 24% of analysts, up 5 points in three months. The revision score is (7)
  • Price: €71.22, 9.6% above the 200-day moving average, which has not risen in any of the last twelve months. Share-price returns are +5.4% over three months, +16.5% over six and (3.1)% over twelve; relative strength is at the 54th percentile
  • Peers: Diageo is rated B on technical and B on sell-side momentum, with a revision score of +11; Rémy Cointreau B and B with +15; Campari D and C with +9. Pernod has the worst revisions in spirits. In the third quarter of 2026, Pernod's consensus fell 3.3% while Diageo's rose 4.6% and Rémy's rose 3.2% (Bernstein)
  • Guidance momentum: none. The last change to guidance was a cut to the medium-term target in August 2026

Inference and so-what. The share price has turned before the estimates. The peer group is turning up and Pernod is last in it, which fits the Sector note's expected order of recovery: Diageo first, Pernod last.

Counter-case

FactSet's weekly series shows FY27 and FY28 consensus up about 1% in the last month, the first rise in a year. The rise comes from currency and is too small to call a turn.

What would change my view

Two months of positive revisions that do not come from currency.

Against the market

None. The market's own behaviour is the evidence here.

Conclusion: momentum is weak in estimates, early in the share price and behind the peers. Momentum leaves step 3 of the case unconfirmed.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. Mixed momentum gives a C, and the price has genuinely turned before the estimates: the shares are 9.6% above the 200-day average and up 16.5% over six months, Buy ratings are up 5 points, and one-month revisions are flat to +1% on currency. I place Pernod at the floor of C rather than moving it to D. The guidance momentum is negative (the medium-term target was cut in August), earnings-per-share revisions are (2)% and (3)% over three and six months, the 200-day average is flat, the dashboard rates technical momentum D, and Pernod has the worst revisions in a peer group that is turning up without it.

#9Riskiness and simplicity

The messageThe case is complex and riskier than average, but most of the risks are slow and visible; the sudden ones sit in India and in trade.

Evidence.

  • The case is not simple. The case needs five things to behave: US shipments, China, India (growth, the listing and the law), the savings, and the balance sheet. The five are linked: the United States and China tend to recover together, and cost cuts work against brand strength
  • Fragilities:
    • Net debt at 3.7 times EBITDA, with the French ten-year government bond yield above 5% and its premium over Germany's at a record
    • A dividend that takes all the free cash flow
    • Indian disputes: a $314 million back-tax demand, an unprovisioned €108 million advertising-tax case, the refusal of a licence in Delhi, and an antitrust inquiry
    • Currency translation that is not hedged
  • Trackability is fair. Monthly US data and quarterly sales show the direction, but China sales to drinkers are hard to verify (Morgan Stanley notes the company's limited record of disclosing them), and US scanner data miss most of the market
  • Suddenness varies. Destocking moves slowly; tariffs, excise and court rulings arrive overnight
  • Precedent. The shares de-rated from 25 times forward earnings in 2021 to 10 times in March 2026 through a run of guidance cuts, with no single collapse. Rémy Cointreau halved its dividend in the current cycle. The Risks report puts the base rate of failure for spirits recovery theses at about 60%, and concludes that cost and cash gains can mask volume decline (its "false friend" verdict). The Risks report dates from June 2026, before the first quarter's improvement

Inference and so-what. The risks are many, mostly slow and mostly visible, with a few sudden ones in India and trade. Viewforth's environment digest warns that a defensive stock carrying leverage de-rates inside a defensive sector, and rates France Double Underweight; Pernod fits both warnings.

Counter-case

With the multiple at the 1st percentile of its range, a good deal of the risk is already in the share price.

What would change my view

The Indian listing, which would remove the debt risk and test the legal risk in public.

Against the market

In February 2026, options priced a 42% chance of a fall below €78; the shares are now at €71, so the market has already travelled much of that path. I think the remaining risk is to earnings and the dividend more than to the multiple.

Conclusion: a complex case with above-average risk, slow-moving in the main and reasonably trackable. The riskiness weakens step 6: the downside case deserves a probability near one in three.

Score: 36, set by the Rater. The memo's range for forward earnings per share in 18 months is EUR 5.50-6.80 around EUR 6.39, about (14)% to +6%, so the range is skewed down. The case needs five linked drivers to behave: US shipments, China, India (growth, the listing and the law), the savings, and the balance sheet. The drivers rest on net debt of 3.8x EBITDA (82nd percentile) and a dividend that takes all the free cash flow, with currency unhedged. Most risks move slowly and the US data are monthly, but China sales to drinkers are hard to verify. Indian tax, licence and antitrust rulings and tariffs or excise can arrive overnight, and the Risks report's base rate for failed spirits recoveries is about 60%. Pernod is a little riskier than D'Ieteren's complex geared holding and less concentrated than Helios Towers.

#10Lifecycle

Evidence. The dashboard's rule puts the stock in the "Broadening" phase. The fundamentals say an earlier phase: earnings per share are at a trough, 26% below FY24; guidance was last cut, not raised; and sell-side momentum is rated F. Only the share price has turned.

Inference and so-what. I place the stock between bottoming and turning up. A thesis broadens when upgrades spread from one driver to several, and Pernod has no upgrades yet. The phase matters for the multiple, because the guideline uses the phase to set the fair multiple.

Counter-case

Prices lead fundamentals. The shares rose 16.5% in six months through poor news, which is how broadening begins.

What would change my view

A guidance raise or a quarter of positive revisions would confirm the turning-up phase. Deeper US destocking at the half-year would put the stock back to bottoming.

Against the market

Jefferies calls the first quarter the trough, and I agree on sales. I differ from the dashboard's label, which reads the share price and not the estimates.

Conclusion: bottoming to turning up, not yet broadening. The lifecycle phase bears on step 5: the setup is at its entry stage, with the clearing of the concern still to be proven.

Score: 48, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo and the computed Bottoming phase rather than the dashboard's Broadening. Earnings per share are at a trough 26% below FY24, guidance was last cut, sell-side momentum is rated F and revisions are still negative, so only the price has turned. The first test of the destocking worry was passed on 15-Oct-26 and the peer group is turning, which makes the phase Bottoming moving towards early Turning up. The 16.5% six-month rise has already taken some of the entry point. That places Pernod just below Solid State and above Linea Directa.

#11The fair multiple

The messageThe guideline fair multiple of 21.87 times is too high a destination for the next 18 months to three years. About 13 times in 18 months and 14.5 times in three years is defensible.

Evidence.

  • Guideline: 21.87 times earnings two years ahead, the 80th percentile of ten years and 85% above today's 11.81 times
  • The stock's own ten-year range: 10th percentile 14.5 times, median 18.6 times, 90th percentile 23.8 times
  • Today's comparisons: Diageo 13.6 times, the Sector median 13.4 times (the 4th percentile of the Sector's own range), Campari 17.4 times

My view. The guideline multiple is too high as a destination for the next 18 months to three years, for four reasons.

  • The lifecycle phase is earlier than the guideline rule assumes (#10), and the guideline calls for a lower multiple in the turning-up phase
  • The history comes from a different business: in the years that set the upper range, sales grew as much as 13% to 21% a year (FY22 and FY23), net debt was about 2.5 times EBITDA, and the sector traded at a 50% premium to the market (2019); the sector now trades at an 11% discount
  • Discount rates are higher, with the US ten-year yield near 5%
  • No forecast in my files restores the old growth rate

The multiple I can defend is about 13 times in 18 months and 14.5 times in three years, rising to 16 to 17 times if organic growth reaches 3% and net debt falls below 3 times EBITDA.

Counter-case

Today's multiple is low on trough earnings, which makes the valuation conservative twice over, and multiples revert quickly once upgrades start.

What would change my view

The Indian listing and a year of 3% organic growth would make the ten-year median of 18.6 times arguable.

Against the market

At 11.8 times, the market is saying that earnings will be cut again. I think 13 to 14.5 times is fair if earnings are merely held, so I am above the market and well below the guideline.

Conclusion: the guideline fair multiple of 21.87 times is reachable only in a full delivery phase that nothing in the evidence yet supports; 13 to 14.5 times is my working range. The fair-multiple judgement bears on step 6: the return at the guideline overstates what the case can deliver on the evidence.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Cheap on both measures gives an A. I place Pernod at the floor of A because much of the cheapness is deserved. The ten-year range was set by a faster-growing, less indebted business when the sector traded at a premium, and the discount to peers only just clears the 15% line and partly reflects the highest debt and worst revisions in the peer group. The business still warrants more than the market pays: the memo defends 13x in 18 months and 14.5x in three years.

End notes

Sources and dates. The latest Earnings Review on file is dated 23-Nov-26 and covers the FY26 results (year to 30-Jun-26, reported 27-Aug-26) and the first-quarter FY27 sales (to 30-Sep-26, reported 15-Oct-26). The financials from FactSet (refreshed 19-Nov-26) show no results reported after the Earnings Review; their last period is the half-year to June 2026, and the next results are the first half of FY27 on 18-Feb-27.

Standard research reports. Change Forces, 23-Nov-26; Business Foundations, 14-Jun-26; Leadership Foundations, 23-Nov-26; Risks, 14-Jun-26. The two June reports pre-date the FY26 results, so the memo uses the Earnings Review and FactSet for everything since.

Bases. Financial history is FactSet's reported basis; consensus is FactSet's (brokers' basis); Viewforth forecasts are from the Financial Analyst's model, update 1. Valuation and price charts are the Master Dashboard's. Charts in visuals/drawn and visuals/drawn-copy-editor are drawn from figures stated in the memo. The Analyst's line-by-line comparison against consensus in #6 is shown as the default table of Viewforth against consensus, from the same model summary.

How the model splits the return (#12). The split is on the return's own basis: the two-year-forward price-to-earnings multiple and two-year-forward earnings per share, today against each horizon. The multiple and earnings parts multiply (1 plus the multiple part, times 1 plus the earnings part, less 1, is the change in the share price); dividends add to that change. The template's own split (TSR Dupont sheet, rows 46 and 47) measures the same return on trailing twelve-month earnings and the trailing multiple: for the 18-month column, +134.0% from the multiple and (16.8)% from earnings; for the three-year column, +124.0% from the multiple and (6.9)% from earnings. The template's split reads differently when earnings over the next twelve months are flat or falling, so the memo uses the split on the return's own basis. The two horizons are the model's fixed columns after the last reported period, so they end on the dates shown, not 18 months and three years from today.

Figures corrected

None. Every figure the memo states about Pernod's past and reported results that the Financial Analyst's model also holds agrees with the model: FY26 revenue of EUR 9,404 million and its (14.2)% growth, FY26 operating profit of EUR 2,423 million and its 25.8% margin, the operating-margin band of 25.8% to 27.6% (the model's FY24 to FY26 margins of 26.9%, 26.9% and 25.8% sit inside it), FY26 earnings per share of EUR 5.85 on the brokers' basis, FY26 free cash flow of EUR 1,197 million, working capital at 77% of sales, and net debt of 3.7 times EBITDA. Figures that the model does not hold, such as the FY23 peak, FY24 earnings per share of EUR 7.90 on the brokers' basis and the organic growth rates, are left as the Analyst wrote them.

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

Minority interests are material: 5.8% of market capitalisation. Our earnings per share are before them; consensus earnings per share are after them.
